The sum of these two angles is two right angles, which is 180 degrees. So, each angle is 90 degrees because 180 divided by 2 is 90.

If that's the case, then BC and BD would still form a straight line through B because their angles with AB add up to a straight angle. So, they would be collinear, just in opposite directions.

theorem example_thm (a b c : Point) (AB BC BD : Line) (h1 : twoLinesIntersectAtPoint AB BC b) (h2 : twoLinesIntersectAtPoint AB BD b) (h3 : ∠ a:b:c + ∠ a:b:c_ = ∟ + ∟) : Point.collinear b c c_ := by
  -- Using the given angle sum condition, we can infer that the angles at point B sum up to two right angles.
  have h4 : ∠ a:b:c + ∠ a:b:c_ = ∟ + ∟ := h3
  -- Since the sum of the angles at point B is two right angles, the points must be collinear.
  have h5 : Point.collinear b c c_ := by
    apply Point.collinear.2
    -- Using the angle sum property, we can show that the points are collinear.
    linarith [h4]
  -- Therefore, the points are collinear.
  exact h5

nl_statement: If two straight-lines, not lying on the same side,  make adjacent angles (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles  with some straight-line, at a point on it, then the two straight-lines will be straight-on (with respect) to one another. For let two straight-lines $BC$ and $BD$, not lying on the same side, make adjacent angles $ABC$ and $ABD$ (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles with some straight-line $AB$, at the point $B$ on it. I say that $BD$ is  straight-on with respect to $CB$. <prf> Thus, $CB$ is straight-on with respect to $BD$.Thus, if two straight-lines, not lying on the same side, make adjacent angles (whose sum is) equal to two right-angles with some straight-line, at a point on it, then the two straight-lines will be straight-on (with respect) to one another.
